newsitem.title: USA: Florida smoker died of lung cancer - medical expert.
newsitem.headline: Florida smoker died of lung cancer - medical expert.

text.p: A medical expert on Thursday showed X-rays of Jean Connor's diseased lungs to jurors in the wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co and said the late smoker had undoubtedly died of lung cancer.

"The patient was clearly and obviously terminally ill. There was no question at the end why she was dying," Dr. Allan Feingold told jurors hearing the lawsuit filed by Connor's family against R.J. Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
Connor's sister, Dana Raulerson, filed the lawsuit on behalf of Connor's estate.

Feingold, chief of pulmonary medicine at South Miami Hospital, spent about five hours on the witness stand as the first and only medical expert for the plaintiffs. He is expected to testify further on Friday.
Feingold, who was not involved in Connor's treatment before she died in October 1995, displayed X-rays of Connor's lungs showing a large mass that he identified as a tumor.

He said it was clear that lung cancer had killed Connor, based on his examination of her medical history. Connor's family contends in the lawsuit that she contracted lung cancer from a three-decade smoking habit.
"She died because of lung cancer," Feingold said.

Feingold said there was no reason to carry out an autopsy on Connor to determine what killed her, countering claims by Reynolds' attorneys in opening arguments that Connor's family, by failing to have an autopsy performed, had deprived jurors of the only definitive way of knowing.
Asked about the possibility of a non-smoker developing lung cancer, Feingold said the chances were "virtually nil."
Earlier in the day, jurors viewed a videotaped deposition of Connor taken in April 1995, six months before she died.
Connor, who looked gaunt and wore a wig, acknowledged that she had seen health warnings on cigarette packages in the late 1960s but said they did not dissuade her from smoking.
"It did not really influence it (her approach to smoking), because it doesn't really tell me anything," Connor said.
Connor was asked about how she viewed her future at that point, six months before her death.
"When you are told you have an illness that cannot be cured, you don't make any plans for the future," she said. "You go from week to week, depending on how you're feeling."
"You don't go buy tickets to go on a cruise six months from now because you may not be alive six months from now. You just don't. It's very difficult to make plans," she said.
